newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 24.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- BANK SET TO KEEP CLOSER EYE ON RISK PROCEDURES

The Bank of England is expected on Monday to announce changes to the way it monitors risk procedures in banks. The move follows criticism of the Bank's supervisory role in high-profile banking crises such as Barings and BCCI. Under the new regime, inspectors will spend more time visiting banks and will be given a more consistent framework for judging whether a bank is running more risks or has fewer controls than its competitors.
-- BRITISH GAS TO FACE LEGAL ACTION BY DATA WATCHDOG

British Gas Trading GAS.L is expected to face legal action this week as a result of attempts to use its 19 million-strong customer database for additional marketing. Centrica, the domestic gas supply business demerged from British Gas, had started to use the 100 million stg database to mail customers asking whether they wished to receive information about additional products. Officials with the data protection watchdog recommended to Elizabeth France, the data protection registrar, that legal action be started against the company over the issue.
-- SWT ADMITS IT DID NOT KEEP ON ENOUGH DRIVERS

South West Trains (SWT), the crisis-hit rail company, has admitted that it could have avoided the cancellations and delays of the past few weeks if it had kept on just 10 more drivers. SWT cut the number of drivers by 71 to 687 in January. In a letter to MPs with constituencies served by SWT, the company's managing director Brian Cox blamed 'implementation problems', including non co-operation from a minority of drivers, for the delays. He also admitted that 'with hindsight' the company should have provided a cushion of a further 10 drivers to cover these problems.
-- DISPUTE THREATENS NAVAL DEFENCE PROGRAMME

The troubled Horizon frigate programme, which involves producing air defence ships for the British, French and Italian navies, is in danger of collapse as an end-of-March deadline to resolve difficulties between the countries will not be met. The UK is unlikely to commit itself to any agreement on the main stumbling block - the capability of the weapons system for the ship - until after the general election. France is keen for progress to be made sooner than that.
-- GERMANY'S CONFIDENCE IN EMU GROWS

A survey of 25,000 German companies, due to be published Monday, reveals that German businesses have become significantly more confident in the past 16 months that a European single currency will start on schedule in January 1999. But the study, from the German chambers of industry and commerce, also found that fewer than one quarter of companies sampled have begun preparations for the introduction of a single currency.
-- BUSINESS CHIEFS 'NOT WORRIED BY BLAIR'

Two polls due to be published Monday will show that most executives in the UK are unworried by the prospect of a change in government, and that their support for the Conservative party is wandering. A survey of almost 750 organizations conducted by Reed Personnel Services found nearly 80 per cent of respondents felt a change of government would either make no difference to their company's prospects or would improve them. And a poll from the Institute of Management found support for the Conservatives dropping to 40 per cent of managers, with support for Labour rising 25 per cent from 13 per cent in 1992.
-- INDUSTRY IS 'ILL-PREPARED' FOR SINGLE CURRENCY

A report due to be published Monday by the 100 Group - the body which comprises 140 finance directors of the largest UK companies - warns that British industry is ill-prepared for the European single currency. The report warns that despite much consideration by companies of the likely impact of the euro, most have not yet made the necessary preparations for it. The report identifies a series of issues businesses must confront regardless of whether the UK joins a single currency, and it stressed the technical problems of converting computer systems to handle the new currency.
-- DIRECTORS MAY SEEK OPT-OUT ON EU WORK RULES

A survey of 700 British companies, conducted for the Institute of Directors and due to be published Monday, reveals that nearly three-quarters of companies are likely to seek exemption from the European Union working time directive when it becomes law in the UK. 74 per cent of respondents say they will claim that the 'nature of their business made compliance impractical', while two-thirds cited the need to perform 'urgent or unforseen work' as justification.
-- C&W SET FOR LAST STAGE OF TELECOMS MERGER

The offer document for the formation and floatation of Cable & Wireless Communications, the 5 billion stg UK cable and telecoms venture, is to be published Monday by telecoms group Cable & Wireless. The venture brings together C&W's Mercury subsidiary and three UK cable companies - Bell CableMedia, Nynex and Videotron. The complex merger is expected to revitalise the UK's stagnant cable television business and inject competition into the telecoms market.
-- PHILIPS TO LIMIT RELIANCE ON NEW PRODUCTS

Dutch consumer electronics giant Philips is to aim for predictability in growth by limiting the extent to which it stakes its future on product breakthroughs. Cor Boonstra, new president of the company, told his first annual meeting of shareholders that shares in Philips were both volatile and had underperformed over the past decade. Announcing the shift away from placing faith in new inventions, he said: 'We are now seeking to break out of this cycle of all-or-nothing offensives and the contrived optimism that accompanies them'.
